x: slug: introduction title: Introduction desc: What ASM Lab 1.45 is, what it simulates, the mining methods it suits, what it is for, how it works and calculates, the ways to build a model, and the conventions used in this manual. Introduction

ASM Lab 1.45 ASM Lab is a mine ventilation program for designing, checking and simulating the ventilation of underground mines. You draw the mine's airways in 3D, or import them from a drawing or another program, place the fans, regulators, walls and doors, and ASM Lab calculates the airflow in every airway. It then goes further than airflow: the temperature and humidity of the air, the gases and dust it carries, and how a fire would spread smoke and heat through the mine. Version 1.45 is the release this manual describes. It brings together everything built into ASM Lab so far: the network solver, the thermal solver, the fire module, the duct module, scripting, the ASM Assistant, the human worker module and the engineering calculators.

What ASM Lab simulates Simulation What you get Airflow The flow m³/s , velocity, pressure drop and air power of every airway, the pressure at every junction, and the operating point of every fan. Temperature and humidity Dry and wet bulb temperature, relative humidity, moisture and heat content along every airway, with heat from the rock, machines, people, blasting and auto compression, and cooling by bulk air coolers. Gases Carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, methane and other gases released in an airway, followed through the network against their exposure limits. Dust Respirable and inhalable dust and diesel particulate matter carried with the air. Fire Heat and smoke carried through the network over time: temperature, oxygen, CO and CO₂ at every place, airflow changes and reversals caused by the fire, and when the smoke first reaches each place. People Heat stress for workers at a stated work rate and clothing, and the human module for stope layouts and evacuation.

Mining methods ASM Lab models any mine whose ventilation can be described as a network of airways joined at junctions, so it is not limited to one mining method. Block and panel caving: extraction level drawpoint drives, undercut levels, ore passes and crusher stations, on several levels joined at the shafts. Bord and pillar: a grid of bords and pillars with walls, brattices and doors between them; the standard wall and door types are included. Narrow reef stoping: inclined stopes between strike drives, with raises and the return airways to the upcast shaft. Sublevel and long hole stoping, and decline mines: ramps, sublevels and stopes, with auxiliary fans and ducts to the headings. Coal seams: several seams in one model, with their own levels and connections.

What ASM Lab is for Planning and design: sizing airways and fans for a new mine or an extension, testing changes before they are built, and comparing options. Checking an operating mine: building the model from survey data, calibrating it against measured airflows, and finding where the air is short or the temperature too high. Emergency preparedness: fire scenarios, escape routes and refuge bays. Monitoring planned : a digital twin of the mine, fed by sensors and machine learning models, so the model follows the mine as it changes.

How ASM Lab works ASM Lab describes the mine as a network . Each excavation the air passes through a drive, a shaft, a raise, a stope is an airway , drawn as its centre line in 3D with a cross section. Airways meet at nodes : a node where airways meet is a junction, and a node at the end of an airway is an end, open to the surface or closed. Each airway has a resistance to airflow, worked out from its length, its cross section and the roughness of its walls the Atkinson friction factor k , plus any shock losses at bends and changes of section. Devices placed on airways add or remove pressure: fans push the air, regulators and walls restrict it. Boundaries tell ASM Lab where air enters and leaves the mine. When you solve, ASM Lab finds the airflow in every airway so that the air entering each junction equals the air leaving it, and the pressure drops around every loop add up to what the fans supply. The thermal solver then follows the air through the network and works out how its temperature and moisture change in each airway. fig A small network in the 3D view with labels: an airway, a junction node, an end node, a fan, a regulator, an intake and an exhaust.

Airway shapes Shape Typical use Rectangular Development drives and crosscuts cut to a square profile. Horseshoe and D shape Drives with an arched roof. Circular Shafts, raise bored raises and ducts. Elliptical and egg shaped Shafts and airways with a non circular rounded section. Trapezoidal Wider at the floor than the roof, as in some drives and coal roadways. Custom Any section you draw or import; its area and perimeter set the resistance.

Airway kinds Every airway has a kind, which sets its default section and colour and lets you find and report airways by what they are: drive, shaft, station, ramp, raise, stope, drawpoint, ore pass and chamber .

Devices and boundaries Item What it does Fan main, booster, auxiliary Adds pressure to its airway along a fan curve pressure, efficiency and power against flow , at a set pressure, or holding a set flow. Regulator Restricts an airway to hold a set flow, a set pressure drop, a set resistance or a set opening. Wall, door, seal, brattice, louvre Closes or restricts an airway; standard types with their resistances are included brick, concrete, shotcrete, good and poor seals, brattice, louvre, rope choke and others . Cooler Cools and dries the air in an airway to a set outlet state or duty. Refuge bay Marks a refuge chamber on an airway, for fire and escape studies. Intake and exhaust Boundaries where air enters or leaves the mine at a given pressure and temperature.

How it calculates Airflow: the square law of resistance pressure drop = R × Q² with Atkinson's friction factor, corrected for air density, solved for the whole network at once by Newton's method; fans follow their curves, corrected for speed and air density by the fan laws. Thermal: the air is followed airway by airway, with heat from the rock from the virgin rock temperature, the age of the airway and the wetness of its walls , auto compression in shafts, machines, people, blasting and coolers; airflow and air density are solved again until both settle. Psychrometry: standard psychrometric equations for mine air at the pressure at each point, the same equations as the calculators. Fire: smoke and heat carried along the airways as the fire grows, with heat lost to the rock walls, and buoyancy and throttling changing the airflow as the fire burns. Stopes and ducts: detailed 2D and 3D flow solvers for a single stope and for duct systems. The equations, their sources and the checks against hand calculations and other programs are in the Solver guide ../../docs/ASM Lab Solver Guide.pdf .

Ways to build a model Draw in 3D: click points in the 3D view to draw airways, shafts and curves, then place devices on them. Import: DXF drawings, JSON network files, spreadsheets of nodes and airways, Datamine files and 3D models. Ask the ASM Assistant: describe what you want in plain words, for example "draw a ramp with two stopes and solve it", and the assistant draws and solves it, then explains the results. Script it: write short JavaScript scripts that draw, change and solve the model, using the functions listed in the Script panel. Python scripting is planned for a later version and will need Python installed on the computer.
Document conventions

Typographical conventions Format Meaning Bold A button, menu, tab, field or other part of the screen, a file name, or text you type. For example: click Solve . Italic Emphasis, or a term explained where it first appears. <angle brackets Text that changes with each use, such as <project name . Do not type the brackets.

Keyboard conventions Key combination Meaning key+key Hold down the first key and press the second. For example, Ctrl+S means hold Ctrl and press S. A single key Press it with the 3D view active. For example, A starts drawing a tunnel.
Menu conventions File Save As means click the File menu, then Save As . Home Create Draw tunnel means the Home tab of the ribbon, the Create group, the Draw tunnel button.

Mouse conventions Action Description Click Press and release the left mouse button. Right click Press and release the right mouse button. While drawing, right click finishes the airway chain. Double click Click the left button twice quickly. Left drag in the 3D view Rotates the view. Right drag in the 3D view Pans the view. Wheel Zooms the view in and out.

slug: interface title: The ASM Lab interface desc: The areas of the window: menus, the ribbon and its tabs, the left and right side bars, the 3D view and its keys, and the solver log and status bar. The ASM Lab interface When a model is open, the ASM Lab window has these areas: 1. Menus: File, Edit, Mine and View. 2. Ribbon: the tabs Home, Design, Duct and Network, each with groups of buttons. 3. Top bar: undo and redo, display modes, the 3D and 2D stope solvers, Downloads, Help, Report bug and Settings. 4. Left side bar: Outliner, Drawing pen, Colour and Clip. 5. 3D view: the mine, with the view tools down its left edge. 6. Right side bar: Inspect, Draw, Network, Solve, Thermal, ASM Assistant and Script. 7. Solver log and status bar: at the bottom of the window. fig The whole ASM Lab window with a sample mine open, numbered 1 to 7 to match the list above.

The ribbon The ribbon holds the commands you use most, grouped by what they do. The Home tab is where you draw, edit and solve. This chapter introduces the ribbon; each button is described where it is used in the chapters that follow. Tab Groups and what they hold Home Create Draw tunnel, Curved tunnel, Add shaft, Place fan, Add regulator, Add wall, Refuge bay, Add cooler ; Edit Duplicate, Merge nodes, Delete, Add node, Remove node, Fillet, Extend ; Simulate Check, Fan curves, Report, Fire, Air use, Charts, Library ; Solve; Navigate; Display Colour by, Label by . Design Create: Split cut an airway at a point , Add stope, Add door / airlock. Duct Auxiliary ventilation: ducts, duct fans, size changes and evasés, with the duct's own 3D and 2D views. Network Boundaries Intake, Exhaust , fans Main fan, Booster, Auxiliary , topology, the network report and exports. Note: Hide ribbon , at the right end of the ribbon, gives the 3D view more room; click a tab to bring the ribbon back. fig The ribbon's Home tab, with the Create, Edit, Simulate, Solve, Navigate and Display groups labelled.
Task: Show and hide the ribbon 1. Click Hide ribbon at the right end of the ribbon. The ribbon closes and the 3D view grows. 2. Click the Home tab to open the ribbon again.

The left side bar Panel What it is for Outliner Everything in the project: files, block models and collections levels . Show, hide, rename, lock or delete them, and choose which collection new drawing goes into. Drawing pen Drawing settings, such as the working elevation new points are drawn at. Colour Colours for drawings, layers and block models. Clip Six cutting planes to slice into the model, for looking inside a level or an orebody. fig The left side bar with the Outliner open, showing a collection and a block model.

The right side bar Panel What it is for Inspect The properties of what you selected: an airway's size, shape, friction factor and device, a node's position and boundary, and their results after a solve. Draw Drawing by typing coordinates, and other drawing dialogues. Network Boundaries and the network checks loose ends, gaps, disconnected parts . Solve Solver settings and the latest solve. Thermal Heat sources and thermal settings for the selected airway or the whole model. ASM Assistant The chat assistant that can draw, solve and explain the model. Script The script editor and the list of script functions. fig The right side bar with the Inspect panel showing a selected airway and its simulation results.

The 3D view The 3D view shows the model. The tools down its left edge fit everything in the view, reset it, and switch the grid, labels, flow arrows and flow animation. Key View 7 Top 1 Front 3 Right 0 Isometric . Frame everything 5 Perspective or orthographic

Solver log and status bar The status bar at the bottom says what ASM Lab is doing and which collection you are drawing in. The solver log above it reports each solve: whether it converged, and any warnings. Click Show to open the full log. fig The bottom of the window after a solve: the status bar and the solver log showing Converged.

slug: files title: File handling desc: The .asmlab project file, opening, importing DXF, spreadsheets and models, saving, exporting, backups, recovering after a crash and cleaning up a model. File handling An ASM Lab project is saved as an .asmlab file. It holds everything: the collections levels , airways, nodes, devices, heat sources, ducts, fire studies, Studio shots and settings. The file is encrypted; you can add a password when you save. Command What it does File New Ctrl+N Starts an empty project. File Open Ctrl+O Opens an .asmlab project or a .json network file. File Import Brings in DXF drawings, 3D models OBJ, STL, glTF , Datamine .dm files and other formats. File Import spreadsheet Reads nodes and airways from an XLSX or CSV file, with a step to match its columns. File Save Ctrl+S Saves the project as an .asmlab file. File Save As Ctrl+Shift+S Saves under a new name or location. File Export JSON, DXF, glTF .glb , Datamine .dm, CSV tables and a PNG screenshot. File Backups The last versions of the project, kept automatically; open one to go back. File Recover Autosave Brings back unsaved work after the program closed unexpectedly. File Revert Discards the changes since t

Task: Save a project 1. Choose File Save , or press Ctrl+S . 2. The first time, choose a folder and type a file name. The file is saved with the extension .asmlab. Note: You can set a password when you save. Keep it safe: a file cannot be opened without its password.
Task: Open a project 1. Choose File Open , or press Ctrl+O . 2. Select an .asmlab file and click Open . The project replaces the one on screen; the one you had is kept in File Backups .

t: Import a DXF drawing as tunnels
x: Task: Import a DXF drawing as tunnels 1. Choose File Import and select the DXF file. Note: ASM Lab reads ASCII DXF files. A binary DXF or a DWG file must first be saved as ASCII DXF in your CAD program. 2. In the Outliner, choose whether the drawing is used as tunnels it becomes a network of airways or kept as a reference drawing. 3. Check the network with Home Simulate Check and fix any gaps it reports before you solve. fig File Import with a DXF drawing loaded, before and after it is used as tunnels.
Task: Recover work after a crash 1. Start ASM Lab again. 2. Choose File Recover Autosave , or click Continue where I left off on the start screen.

slug: settings title: Settings desc: The Settings window: theme, display, geothermal, engineering, regulatory limits and import and export options. Settings Open the settings with Settings at the top right, or File Settings . The settings apply to the whole program; settings that belong to one model, such as the site's surface conditions, are saved in its project file. Section What you set Theme Light or dark appearance. Display Colours, labels, line widths and how results are shown in the 3D view. Geothermal Rock properties and the virgin rock temperature with depth, for the thermal solver; presets for common regions. Engineering Engineering choices for the solver, such as the air density basis and the solver tolerance. Regulatory The limits results are checked against: minimum and maximum air velocities, wet bulb and gas limits. Import / Export Units and options used when reading and writing files. fig The Settings window open on the Regulatory section. Note: The limits under Regulatory are starting values. Set them to your mine's own standards and your country's regulations.

slug: first mine title: Drawing your first mine desc: Step by step from an empty project to a solved mine: an intake shaft, a level, a return shaft with a main fan, boundaries, checking, solving, reading the results and saving. Drawing your first mine In this chapter you draw a small mine from nothing: an intake shaft, a level with two drives, a return shaft with a main fan. Then you solve it and read the results. It takes about fifteen minutes.
Task: Start a new project 1. Start ASM Lab. On the start screen, click New model . 2. A new, empty collection is made and the 3D view shows the grid. fig The start screen with New model highlighted.

Task: Draw the intake shaft 1. Click Home Create Add shaft . 2. A shaft is drawn like a tunnel, with two clicks: click the top of the shaft, move the cursor down a trail shows the shaft and click its bottom. 3. In the Inspect panel, check the shaft's diameter and friction factor. fig A shaft just drawn and selected, with its properties in the Inspect panel.

Task: Draw the level 1. Open the Drawing pen on the left side bar and set the Working elevation to the depth of the bottom of the shaft. 2. Click Home Create Draw tunnel , or press A . 3. Click the bottom of the shaft to start, then click each point along the drive. Each click adds a node; points snap to the grid and to existing nodes. 4. Right click to finish the drive. 5. Draw the second drive in the same way, from the end of the first to where the return shaft will be. 6. Select a drive and set its width, height and shape in the Inspect panel. fig Drawing a drive: the clicked points and the preview line to the cursor.

t: Draw the return shaft and add the main fan
x: Task: Draw the return shaft and add the main fan 1. Draw a second shaft from the end of the level up to the surface. 2. Click Home Create Place fan and choose Main fan . 3. Click the return shaft. An arrow shows the direction the fan blows; click the side the air goes to, towards the surface for an exhausting fan. 4. In the Inspect panel, choose a fan from the library or enter its curve. fig The main fan on the return shaft with its direction arrow.
Task: Set the intake and exhaust 1. Click Network Intake and click the top node of the intake shaft. 2. Click Network Exhaust and click the top node of the return shaft.

Task: Check and solve 1. Click Home Simulate Check . ASM Lab lists anything that would stop a solve, such as a loose end or a missing boundary. Fix each one. 2. Press F5 , or click Solve . 3. The solver log reports Converged . fig The Check window with no problems, and the solver log after a converged solve.

Task: Read the results 1. In Display , set Colour by to Velocity . The legend shows the range. 2. Click an airway. The Inspect panel shows its flow, pressure drop, velocity and velocity pressure under Simulation Results. 3. Click the fan's airway to see the fan's operating point: flow, total and static pressure, air and shaft power and efficiency. 4. Click the play button on the left of the 3D view to watch the air move. fig The solved mine coloured by velocity, with an airway selected and its results in the Inspect panel.
Task: Save the mine 1. Choose File Save and name the project My first mine . You have drawn, solved and saved a mine. The next chapters describe each part of ASM Lab in more detail.

x: slug: ex airflow title: Worked examples: airflow, pressure and regulators desc: Course questions on pitot tubes, airways in parallel, regulators and booster fans, solved by hand and with the ASM Lab network solver, with the error against the memo. Worked examples: airflow, pressure and regulators The questions come from the MINN3019A mine ventilation course tutorials, class calculations, self study problems and lecture slides . Each one is set out as the question, the hand solution as in the memo, and then the same question answered with ASM Lab, with the difference from the memo. Memo values read off psychrometric charts carry the chart's reading accuracy, about 0.3 kJ/kg on sigma heat and 0.2 °C on a temperature, so differences of that size are reading differences, not errors.

t: Pitot tube in an air pipe
c: Worked examples: airflow, pressure and regulators
x: Pitot tube in an air pipe Tutorial 1, question 2. A pitot tube is installed at the midpoint of a 250 mm air pipe. The velocity pressure measured on a manometer is 8 mm water and the static pressure 6 mm water. The air temperature is 21 °C and the barometric pressure 744 mm mercury. The flow is turbulent and the average velocity is 82 % of the velocity at the centre of the pipe. Calculate the volume flow and the mass flow of the air. Take g = 9.79 m/s², mercury 13 550 kg/m³ and water 1 000 kg/m³, and treat air as an ideal gas.

c: Worked examples: airflow, pressure and regulators
x: Hand solution The barometric pressure and the density of dry air: = p = ρ_Hg g h = 13 550 × 9.79 × 0.744 = 98 692 Pa = ρ = p / R T = 98 692 / 287 × 294.15 = 1.17 kg/m³ The velocity pressure and the centre line velocity: = VP = ρ_w g h = 1 000 × 9.79 × 0.008 = 78.3 Pa = u = √ 2 VP / ρ = √ 2 × 78.3 / 1.17 = 11.6 m/s The average velocity, the volume flow and the mass flow: = u_avg = 0.82 × 11.6 = 9.5 m/s = Q = u_avg × π D² / 4 = 9.5 × 0.049 = 0.465 m³/s = m = ρ Q = 1.17 × 0.5 = 0.585 kg/s the memo rounds Q to 0.5 first Answer: Q = 0.465 m³/s say 0.5 m³/s ; m = 0.585 kg/s in the memo.

c: Worked examples: airflow, pressure and regulators
x: With ASM Lab

c: Worked examples: airflow, pressure and regulators
x: Task: Answer it with the calculators 1. Open Tools Calculators and choose Psychrometry . Enter 98.69 kPa, a dry bulb of 21 °C and a relative humidity of 0 %. The dry air density is 1.169 kg/m³. 2. Choose Velocity pressure . Enter the density and change the velocity until the velocity pressure reads 78.3 Pa: 11.58 m/s. 3. The rest is the area and the 0.82 factor: Q = 0.466 m³/s, m = 0.545 kg/s. Quantity Memo ASM Lab Error Air density kg/m³ 1.170 1.169 0.09 % Centre line velocity m/s 11.60 11.58 0.21 % Average velocity m/s 9.50 9.49 0.08 % Volume flow m³/s 0.465 0.466 0.21 % Mass flow kg/s 0.585 0.545 6.90 % Note: The mass flow differs by 7 % because the memo multiplies by Q rounded to 0.5 m³/s. With the unrounded 0.465 m³/s the hand answer is 1.17 × 0.465 = 0.544 kg/s, the same as ASM Lab.

t: Two crosscuts in parallel: doors, regulator and booster fan
c: Worked examples: airflow, pressure and regulators
x: Two crosscuts in parallel: doors, regulator and booster fan Class calculations 1, question 1. Two crosscuts lead from a sub vertical shaft to a stoping section. The upper crosscut AD is 3.0 m × 3.0 m and 400 m long. All the air, 80 m³/s, now flows in the lower crosscut ABCD, and the pressure across the doors in the upper crosscut is 1.05 kPa. The air density is 1.25 kg/m³. 1. What quantity flows in each crosscut if the doors are left open? 2. What size of regulator in the upper crosscut sends 60 m³/s through ABCD? 3. Keeping the pressure available unchanged, what booster fan in the lower crosscut keeps 20 m³/s in the upper one?

c: Worked examples: airflow, pressure and regulators
x: Hand solution The resistance of ABCD at the prevailing density, from the door pressure, and of AD from its size with an assumed k factor of 0.018 Ns²/m⁴: = R_ABCD = p / Q² = 1 050 / 80² = 0.1641 Ns²/m⁸ = R_AD = k C L / A³ = 0.018 × 12 × 400 / 9³ = 0.11852 Ns²/m⁸ a With the doors open the two are in parallel: = 1/√R_T = 1/√0.11852 + 1/√0.1641, so R_T = 0.03464 Ns²/m⁸ = p = R_T Q² = 0.03464 × 80² = 221.7 Pa = Q_AD = √ p / R_AD = √ 221.7 / 0.11852 = 43.25 m³/s; Q_ABCD = 80 − 43.25 = 36.75 m³/s b For 60 m³/s in ABCD the circuit needs R_ABCD × 60² = 591 Pa, while 20 m³/s in AD uses only R_AD × 20² = 47.4 Pa. The regulator takes the difference, 543.6 Pa: = A = 1.2 Q √ ρ / p = 1.2 × 20 × √ 1.25 / 543.6 = 1.15 m² c Keeping 221.7 Pa across the circuit, the regulator now takes 221.7 − 47.4 = 174.3 Pa A = 2.03 m² and a booster in ABCD supplies the rest of the 591 Pa: = p_booster = 591 − 221.7 = 369.3 Pa at 60 m³/s Answer: a 43.3 and 36.8 m³/s; b a 1.2 m² regulator; c a 2 m² regulator and a booster of 60 m³/s at 369 Pa.

c: Worked examples: airflow, pressure and regulators
x: With ASM Lab

t: Build the two crosscuts as a network
c: Worked examples: airflow, pressure and regulators
x: Task: Build the two crosscuts as a network 1. Draw the two crosscuts between the same two nodes and give them the resistances above in the Inspect panel Resistance override . 2. a Put a fan set to Fixed quantity , 80 m³/s, on the shaft airway and press F5 . The solver splits the air: 43.24 m³/s in AD and 36.76 m³/s in ABCD, at 221.6 Pa. 3. b Add a regulator to AD in target pressure drop mode with 543.6 Pa. ASM Lab sizes it at 1.151 m². Set that area, solve again, and ABCD carries 60.00 m³/s. 4. c Set the shaft to a fixed pressure difference of 221.7 Pa, give AD a regulator of 2.03 m² and put a Fixed quantity booster of 60 m³/s in ABCD. The solver reports the booster pressure, 369.0 Pa, with 20.00 m³/s left in AD. slug: ex fans title: Worked examples: fans desc: Course questions on main fan duty, the fan laws, density changes and evasés, solved by hand and with ASM Lab, with fan charts and the error against the memo. Worked examples: fans The questions come from the MINN3019A mine ventilation course tutorials, class calculations, self study problems and lecture slides . Each one is set out as the question, the hand solution as in the memo, and then the same question answered with ASM Lab, with the difference from the memo. Memo values read off psychrometric charts carry the chart's reading accuracy, about 0.3 kJ/kg on sigma heat and 0.2 °C on a temperature, so differences of that size are reading differences, not errors.

t: Main fan duty for a mine
x: Main fan duty for a mine Tutorial 4. The downcast shaft 1–2 is 6 m in diameter with an air velocity of 11 m/s and an air density of 1.05 kg/m³. The upcast 7–10 is 5.0 m in diameter. The air splits at 3 into two equal routes, 3–4–5–6 and 3–8–9–6, which join at 6. Ignore the resistance of the mining areas 4–5 and 8–9 , compressed air and leakage. The air density in the fan drift is 1.02 kg/m³. Calculate a the air volume at the main fans and b the pressure rating of the main fans.

Hand solution Every resistance underground is first corrected to the fan drift density R × 1.02 / ρ_local . The corrected values are 1–2: 0.00486, 2–3: 0.03709, 3–4 and 3–8: 0.04098, 5–6 and 9–6: 0.03778, 6–7: 0.00297 and 7–10: 0 Ns²/m⁸. = Series 1–3: 0.00486 + 0.03709 = 0.04195 Ns²/m⁸ = Each route 3–6: 0.04098 + 0 + 0.03778 = 0.07876 Ns²/m⁸; the two in parallel: 0.07876 / 4 = 0.01969 Ns²/m⁸ = Mine: R_T = 0.04195 + 0.01969 + 0.00297 = 0.06461 Ns²/m⁸ The mass flow in the downcast is carried to the fan drift: = Q_dc = 11 × π × 6² / 4 = 311 m³/s; m = 1.05 × 311 = 326.6 kg/s = Q_fan = 326.6 / 1.02 = 320.2 m³/s = P_fan = R_T Q² = 0.06461 × 320.2² = 6 624 Pa Answer: a 320.2 m³/s; b 6.6 kPa at 1.02 kg/m³.
With ASM Lab

t: Solve the mine for its fan duty
x: Task: Solve the mine for its fan duty 1. Draw the ten nodes and the airways and give each airway its corrected resistance Resistance override in Inspect . 2. Put the main fan on 7–10 and set it to Fixed quantity , 320.2 m³/s. 3. Press F5 . The fan reports the pressure it needs, 6 621 Pa, and each route carries 162.5 m³/s. Quantity Memo ASM Lab Error Air volume at the fan m³/s 320.2 320.2 0.01 % Fan pressure Pa 6 624 6 621 0.05 % Note: ASM Lab reports the pressure of a fan with no curve set to a fixed quantity from version 1.45. Earlier versions showed 0 Pa for such a fan.

t: The fan laws: changing the speed
x: The fan laws: changing the speed Lecture slides, fan graphs with density and speed. A fan tested at 11.5 r/s and 1.2 kg/m³ gives the curve below. Re plot the pressure and power curves at 13.8 r/s. Q m³/s P Pa Power kW 0 1 770 8.7 2 1 820 12.3 4 1 910 15.0 6 1 670 16.5 8 1 090 16.0 9 610 15.0 10 0 13.0

Hand solution At a constant density the quantity varies with the speed, the pressure with its square and the power with its cube; the efficiency stays the same at corresponding points: = n₂ / n₁ = 13.8 / 11.5 = 1.2 = Q₂ = 1.2 Q₁, P₂ = 1.2² P₁ = 1.44 P₁, W₂ = 1.2³ W₁ = 1.728 W₁ So 4 m³/s at 1 910 Pa and 15 kW becomes 4.8 m³/s at 2 750.4 Pa and 25.92 kW, and so on down the table.
With ASM Lab

t: Run the fan at a new speed
x: Task: Run the fan at a new speed 1. Enter the 11.5 r/s curve as the fan's points with a reference speed of 11.5 r/s, and set the operating speed to 13.8 r/s. 2. To check a point of the new curve, give the system the resistance that passes through it R = P / Q² and solve. The fan settles exactly on the memo's re plotted point. chart ex fan laws.svg The fan at 11.5 r/s and the curve re plotted at 13.8 r/s, with ASM Lab's operating points on four system curves. t: A fan tested on surface and used underground
x: A fan tested on surface and used underground Lecture slides, density change tutorial. A direct driven axial fan is tested on surface at an air density of 1.01 kg/m³. It is to be used underground where the density is 1.26 kg/m³, on a 760 mm ventilation column 54 m long with a k factor of 0.0035 Ns²/m⁴. Find the operating point, input power and efficiency. Q m³/s P Pa Input power kW 0 930 3.6 2 840 4.6 4 870 5.9 6 910 7.8 8 860 10.0 10 730 12.4 12 490 14.7 14 0 14.6

Hand solution At a constant speed the quantity stays, and the pressure and power scale with the density: = P₂ = P₁ × 1.26 / 1.01 = 1.2475 P₁; W₂ = 1.2475 W₁ The column resistance k taken at 1.2 kg/m³ and corrected to 1.26 kg/m³ : = A = π × 0.76² / 4 = 0.4536 m²; C = π × 0.76 = 2.388 m = R = k C L / A³ × 1.26 / 1.2 = 0.0035 × 2.388 × 54 / 0.4536³ × 1.05 = 5.075 Ns²/m⁸ The operating point is where R Q² meets the new fan curve, between 10 and 12 m³/s. Interpolating along the curve: = Q = 11.56 m³/s, P = 678 Pa, input power = 17.7 kW = η = Q P / W = 11.56 × 678 / 1 000 / 17.7 = 44.2 % Answer: about 11.6 m³/s at 678 Pa, 17.7 kW and 44 % efficiency. The slides give no numerical answer, so the hand answer here is the reference.

t: An evasé on the fan discharge
x: An evasé on the fan discharge Lecture slides, fan performance in a system. An 85 % efficient evasé with an inlet area of 0.5 m² and an outlet area of 1.2 m² is fitted to the discharge of an axial fan. Plot the new fan characteristic at 1.2 kg/m³.

Hand solution The evasé turns part of the velocity pressure at the fan outlet into useful pressure: = gain = η VP_in − VP_out = 0.85 × ½ ρ Q / 0.5 ² − Q / 1.2 ² At 6 m³/s: VP_in = 0.6 × 12² = 86 Pa, VP_out = 0.6 × 5² = 15 Pa, gain = 0.85 × 71 = 61 Pa, so the fan with the evasé gives 500 + 61 = 561 Pa.

slug: ex psychrometry title: Worked examples: psychrometry and heat desc: Course questions on mixing air streams, heat absorption capacity, auto compression in a deep shaft and pump chamber heat, solved with charts and with ASM Lab. t: Mixing return air with intake air
x: Mixing return air with intake air Tutorial 2, question 1. The air entering a stope must not have a wet bulb above 29 °C. 20 m³/s of return air is available at 32 °C saturated, and intake air at 26.7/32.2 °C. The barometric pressure is 100 kPa. How much intake air must be mixed with the return air?

Hand solution From the 100 kPa chart: return air sigma heat 107.2 kJ/kg and specific volume 0.92 m³/kg; intake air 81.5 kJ/kg and 0.906 m³/kg; the mixture at 29 °C wet bulb 92.2 kJ/kg. = m_return = 20 / 0.92 = 21.75 kg/s = A × 81.5 + 21.75 × 107.2 = A + 21.75 × 92.2, so A = 30.4 kg/s = Q = 30.4 × 0.906 = 27.5 m³/s Answer: 27.5 m³/s of intake air.
With ASM Lab

t: Find the intake quantity with the mixing calculator
x: Task: Find the intake quantity with the mixing calculator 1. Open Tools Calculators Air mixing at 100 kPa. Stream 1: 32/32 °C, 20 m³/s. Stream 2: 26.7/32.2 °C. 2. Change the quantity of stream 2 until the mixture's wet bulb is 29.0 °C: 29.0 m³/s. Quantity Memo ASM Lab Error Sigma heat, return air kJ/kg 107.2 107.4 0.19 % Sigma heat, intake air kJ/kg 81.5 81.8 0.39 % Sigma heat, mixture kJ/kg 92.2 92.2 0.01 % Specific volume, return air m³/kg 0.920 0.920 0.04 % Intake air mass kg/s 30.4 32.0 5.34 % Intake air volume m³/s 27.5 29.0 5.38 % Note: Every property agrees with the chart to its reading accuracy, yet the quantity differs by about 5 %. The answer hangs on the difference between the mixture and the intake sigma heat, only 10.7 kJ/kg, so reading the intake air as 81.5 instead of 81.82 kJ/kg alone moves the answer by 3 %. The same sigma heat balance with ASM Lab's property values gives 28.8 m³/s, and the exact mix, which keeps the enthalpy and the moisture, 29.0 m³/s.

t: Pump chamber air: to return, or back into the intake?
x: Pump chamber air: to return, or back into the intake? Tutorial 2, question 2. 75 m³/s of intake air at 18/26 °C passes a pump chamber; 13 m³/s of it ventilates the chamber, where 70 % of the pumps' 1 000 kW goes into the air. The return wet bulb from the section must not exceed 32 °C, and the barometric pressure is 100 kPa. Scheme 1 sends the pump chamber air straight to return; scheme 2 lets it rejoin the intake. What is the heat absorption capacity of the air for the section in each scheme, and which is better?

Hand solution From the 100 kPa chart: intake air 50.2 kJ/kg and 0.873 m³/kg; return at 32 °C saturated 107.2 kJ/kg. = Scheme 1: m = 62 / 0.873 = 71 kg/s; capacity = 71 × 107.2 − 50.2 = 4 050 kW = Scheme 2: m = 75 / 0.873 = 85.9 kg/s; capacity = 85.9 × 57 − 700 = 4 200 kW Answer: scheme 1 4 050 kW, scheme 2 4 200 kW; scheme 2 is better by about 150 kW.

t: A deep downcast shaft and a haulage
x: A deep downcast shaft and a haulage Tutorial 3. 300 m³/s of air at 13.6/20.0 °C enters an 1 800 m deep downcast shaft at 84.7 kPa. In the shaft the air picks up 1.15 kJ/kg per 300 m of heat and 0.5 g/kg per 200 m of moisture from the surroundings; auto compression adds 9.79 kJ/kg per 1 000 m. At the bottom 105 kPa it travels 1 600 m along a haulage, picking up 2 890 kW of heat and 1.8 l/s of water. Find the condition of the air at the end of the haulage and the share of the shaft's heat that comes from auto compression.

Hand solution At the shaft top 85 kPa chart : r = 9.0 g/kg, S = 42.4 kJ/kg, mass flow 297.6 kg/s. = Auto compression: 9.79 × 1.8 = 17.62 kJ/kg; heat from the rock: 1.15 × 1 800 / 300 = 6.9 kJ/kg = Moisture in the shaft: 0.5 × 1 800 / 200 = 4.5 g/kg = Haulage: 2 890 / 297.6 = 9.71 kJ/kg and 1 800 / 297.6 = 6.05 g/kg = End of haulage: S = 42.4 + 17.62 + 6.9 + 9.71 = 76.63 kJ/kg, r = 9.0 + 4.5 + 6.05 = 19.55 g/kg = From the 105 kPa chart: 26.1/28.8 °C = Auto compression: 297.6 × 17.62 = 5 244 kW, which is 17.62 / 24.52 = 71.9 % of the shaft's heat Answer: 26.1/28.8 °C at the end of the haulage; auto compression 5 244 kW, 71.9 % of the heat added in the shaft.

t: Heat from pumps and rock in a crosscut
x: Heat from pumps and rock in a crosscut Class calculations 1, question 2. 55.3 m³/s of air at 29.1/35.3 °C enters 56 level crosscut at A 117.5 kPa . Part of it ventilates a pump chamber with four 1 500 kW pumps whose motors are 94 % efficient, and then rejoins the main stream at B. At the end of the crosscut, C, the air is at 31.1/34.8 °C. Find a the temperature at B, assuming no moisture is added, and b the heat from the rock and the moisture picked up between A and C.

Hand solution From the 117.5 kPa chart at A: S = 82.8 kJ/kg, r = 19.3 g/kg, 0.778 m³/kg, so m = 55.3 / 0.778 = 71.1 kg/s. = Pump heat: 4 × 1 500 / 0.94 − 1 500 = 383 kW, so ΔS = 383 / 71.1 = 5.4 kJ/kg = S_B = 82.8 + 5.4 = 88.2 kJ/kg at r = 19.3 g/kg: 30.3/40.3 °C = At C: S = 91.5 kJ/kg, r = 23.3 g/kg; heat A to C = 71.1 × 8.7 = 618.6 kW = Heat from the rock: 618.6 − 383 = 236 kW; water: 71.1 × 23.3 − 19.3 = 284 g/s = 0.284 l/s Answer: a 30.3/40.3 °C at B; b 236 kW from the rock and 0.284 l/s of water.
With ASM Lab

t: Plant duty, positional efficiency and condenser water
x: Plant duty, positional efficiency and condenser water Refrigeration self study problem 1. An underground system: chilled water 35.1 l/s entering the evaporator at 17.2 °C and leaving at 8.9 °C; 30.4 m³/s of air through the cooling coils, in at 31.8/33.9 °C and out at 27.5/27.5 °C, at 110 kPa; condenser water in at 38.4 °C and out at 44.3 °C; actual compressor COP 3.8. Find the plant duty, the positional efficiency and the condenser water flow.

Hand solution = Plant duty = evaporator duty = 35.1 × 4.187 × 17.2 − 8.9 = 1 220 kW = From the 110 kPa chart: S_in = 99.3, S_out = 79.9 kJ/kg, v = 0.836 m³/kg, so m = 30.4 / 0.836 = 36.4 kg/s = Coil duty = 36.4 × 99.3 − 79.9 = 706.2 kW; positional efficiency = 706.2 / 1 220 = 57.9 % = Compressor work = 1 220 / 3.8 = 321 kW; condenser duty = 1 541 kW = Condenser water = 1 541 / 4.187 × 44.3 − 38.4 = 62.4 l/s Answer: 1 220 kW; 57.9 %; 62.4 l/s.
With ASM Lab

An underground cooling plant Refrigeration self study problem 4. Pump power at the cooling coil outlet 60 kW; line losses 160 kW from the evaporator to the coils and 95 kW back; evaporator at 5.9 °C, condenser at 46.1 °C; 50.0 m³/s of air into the coils at 29.0/35.0 °C, out at 23.0/23.0 °C, at 105 kPa; condenser water pump 80 kW; compressor motor 90 % efficient with an input of 583 kW. Find the plant duty, positional efficiency, overall COP, heat rejected in the tower, Carnot COP and overall cycle efficiency.

Hand solution = From the 105 kPa chart: S_in = 89.1, S_out = 64.9 kJ/kg, v = 0.872 m³/kg, so m = 50 / 0.872 = 57.3 kg/s = Coil duty = 57.3 × 89.1 − 64.9 = 1 385 kW = Plant duty = 1 385 + 60 + 160 + 95 = 1 700 kW; positional efficiency = 1 385 / 1 700 = 81.5 % = Overall COP = 1 700 / 583 = 2.9 = Heat rejected = 1 700 + 0.9 × 583 + 80 + 60 = 2 365 kW = Carnot COP = 273.15 + 5.9 / 46.1 − 5.9 = 6.9; overall cycle efficiency = 2.9 / 6.9 = 42 % Answer: 1 700 kW; 81.5 %; 2.9; 2 365 kW; 6.9; 42 %.
With ASM Lab
